course.title: Track 3: The Industry Map
course.description: Protect your rights, register properly with collection societies, and avoid the common legal traps that cost independent artists money.
objectives: Understand the two copyrights in every recorded song
Use split sheets to prevent ownership disputes
Register with a PRO so your performance royalties actually reach you
Read management and record deal terms without being taken advantage of

lessons.title: Copyrights 101 — The Two Halves of a Song
lessons.content:
The music business is entirely built on copyright law. If you do not understand this, you will be exploited. It is that simple. Every single piece of recorded music generates two distinct copyrights.

**The Master (sound recording).** This is the actual audio file you listen to — the specific recording, the exact performance, the exact production. Historically, record labels owned the Master because they paid for the studio time.

**The Composition (publishing).** This is the underlying song — the lyrics, the melody, the chord progression. It is the idea of the song before it is ever recorded. Songwriters and publishers own this.

Here is a real-world example that makes it crystal clear. Dolly Parton wrote "I Will Always Love You", so she owns the Composition. Whitney Houston later recorded a cover, and Whitney's label owns the Master of that specific recording. But Dolly still gets paid for the Composition every single time Whitney's version is played on the radio, streamed, or used in a film — reportedly over $10 million from that version alone, without singing a note on it.

As an independent artist writing and recording your own music, you own 100% of both copyrights. Do not give them away lightly. Understand what you are signing before you sign anything.

assignment.title: Identify Who Owns Your Track
assignment.instructions: Identify who owns the master and the publishing for your chosen track. Are you the sole writer? Did you buy a beat from a producer online? If so, review that beat licence and note what rights you actually hold — exclusive or non-exclusive, and whether the producer takes a publishing percentage.

lessons.title: Split Sheets and Collaboration
lessons.content:
Music is collaborative. You might write the lyrics, someone else writes the guitar riff, and a producer builds the beat. When the song starts making money, who owns what percentage of the Composition?

If you do not decide this in writing immediately, the law in many territories assumes an equal split among everyone present in the creative session, regardless of who did the most work. That leads to bitter disputes, broken friendships, and expensive lawsuits once the song generates revenue.

The solution is a **split sheet** — a simple written agreement, signed by all collaborators, stating exactly what percentage of the song's composition each person owns. It includes everyone's full legal name, their PRO affiliation, their publisher if they have one, the exact percentage they own, and the date and song title.

**Rule of thumb:** have the conversation about splits before you leave the studio or finalise the file transfer. It is a sign of professionalism, not greed. The best time to discuss money is when everyone is happy and excited about the song. The worst time is six months later when it is taking off and everyone remembers their contribution differently.

assignment.title: Complete a Split Sheet
assignment.instructions: Complete a split sheet for your track. Even if you wrote and produced 100% of it yourself, download a free template and fill it out. Build the muscle memory of treating your art as a legal asset from day one.

lessons.title: PROs and Royalties
lessons.content:
When your song is played on the radio, streamed, used in a TV show, performed at a live venue, or even played over the speakers in a coffee shop, it generates a **public performance royalty** for the composition.

But how do you actually collect that money? You cannot personally monitor every radio station and coffee shop in the world. That is where a **Performance Rights Organization** comes in.

In the United States the main PROs are ASCAP and BMI. In the United Kingdom it is PRS for Music. Other territories have equivalents — SOCAN in Canada, APRA AMCOS in Australia. These organisations hold agreements with broadcasters, venues and streaming platforms. They monitor public performances, collect the royalties owed, and distribute the money to registered songwriters and publishers.

If you are not registered with a PRO, your performance royalties sit in a black box, unclaimed. Eventually that unclaimed money is redistributed to other registered artists. You are literally leaving money on the table.

assignment.title: Register With a PRO
assignment.instructions: Register as a writer AND a publisher with a Performance Rights Organization in your territory. If you do not have a publisher, register as your own publishing company — you will typically need a Tax ID and/or an LLC to validate it. Once registered as both, register each song you write so the PRO collects 100% of the royalties on your behalf. Report which PRO you joined and what is still outstanding.

lessons.title: Contracts and Management
lessons.content:
As you grow, people will want to work with you — managers, labels, publishers, booking agents. This is exciting, but you need to understand the standard terms so you do not sign your life away in a moment of excitement.

**Artist managers.** A manager is your business partner. They handle the logistics — booking shows, negotiating deals, managing your schedule — so you can focus on the art. The industry standard commission is **15% to 20% of your gross income**. A good manager earns that many times over. A bad one takes 20% and does nothing. Always ask: what specifically will you do for me that I cannot do myself right now?

**Record deals and advances.** If a label offers you a $50,000 advance, that is not a signing bonus and it is not free money. It is a **loan against your future royalties**. The label keeps 100% of your royalty earnings until that $50,000 — plus all marketing, recording and video costs they spent on your behalf — is entirely paid back. This is called recoupment. Only once the label has recouped every penny will you see another royalty cheque. Many artists never recoup.

As an independent artist, you are the label. You fund the project yourself, even if that is $0 using free tools, but you keep 100% of the profits from day one. There is no one to recoup.

**Toolkit for Track 3.** Songtrust and Symphonic offer free downloadable split sheet templates. ASCAP and BMI are free for writers to join. HelloSign has a free tier for electronic signatures on contracts and split sheets.

assignment.title: Study a Management Agreement
assignment.instructions: Find a standard artist management agreement template online and read it through, just to familiarise yourself with the language, the standard clauses, and what to watch for. Note the three clauses you found most surprising or concerning.

lessons.title: Track 3 Quiz
lessons.content: You have covered copyright, split sheets, performance royalties and contract basics. Answer the questions below to confirm you are ready for Track 4.

questions.prompt: What are the two distinct copyrights generated by every piece of recorded music?

options.text: The Master (sound recording) and the Composition (publishing / underlying song)
The digital copyright and the physical copyright
The domestic copyright and the international copyright
The artist's copyright and the producer's copyright

questions.explanation: The Master is the specific recording. The Composition is the underlying song — lyrics, melody, chords. They can be owned by different people.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a split sheet?

options.text: It divides streaming revenue between the artist and the distributor
It is a written agreement signed by all collaborators stating what percentage of a song's composition each person owns
It splits a long song into separate tracks for release
It records how studio costs will be shared

questions.explanation: Without one, many territories assume an equal split among everyone in the room — regardless of who actually did the work.

questions.prompt: What does a Performance Rights Organization (PRO) do?

options.text: It books live performances on behalf of artists
It distributes your music to streaming platforms
It collects and distributes royalties to songwriters and publishers whenever their compositions are performed publicly
It registers your trademark and artist name

questions.explanation: Radio, TV, live venues, streaming, even a coffee shop — the PRO monitors, collects, and pays out to registered writers and publishers.

questions.prompt: What is the standard industry commission rate for an artist manager?

options.text: 5% to 10% of gross income
15% to 20% of gross income
30% to 40% of gross income
50% of gross income

questions.explanation: 15% to 20% of gross is standard. Always ask what they will do that you cannot do yourself right now.

questions.prompt: In a traditional record deal, what is an "advance"?

options.text: A signing bonus the artist keeps regardless of performance
A loan against future royalties that must be fully recouped before the artist earns anything further
A payment made to the artist's manager on signing
A grant from a PRO to fund recording costs

questions.explanation: The label recoups the advance plus marketing, recording and video costs out of your royalties before you see another cheque. Many artists never recoup.
